title: Visit five of her back program, and something has changed
objective: Report to the supervising PT any new red-flag feature in a patient with back pain, such as signs of cauda equina or cord compression, infection, fracture or malignancy, before continuing treatment
secondaryObjectives: Recognizing when a patient's response to treatment requires reporting back to the supervising PT
Implementing therapeutic exercise and manual therapy per a PT's established plan of care
Documenting musculoskeletal treatment sessions and progress toward established goals

brief.situation: 15:00 in an outpatient orthopedic clinic. You are the physical therapist assistant, carrying out the physical therapist's plan of care. Ms. Alvarez, 52, is on visit 5 of 8 for low back pain with left leg pain from a disc herniation. Last visit she was improving.
handover: Plan of care (written by Dr. Kim, PT, at the evaluation 2 weeks ago): core stabilization progression, prone press-ups, mechanical lumbar traction 15 min, home program. Reexamination at visit 8.
The plan's red-flag screen at every visit: bladder, bowel and saddle sensation, and any new weakness or numbness.
Dr. Kim is in the building today, seeing a patient in the next room. Clinic policy: stop and report any new red flag to the PT before going on; the PT reexamines and decides where the patient goes.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Each question or measure takes the time on its button. Decide what to collect, what it means for today's session and who needs to know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

A question set or a data-collection measure: about 1 min.
The check-in at the start of a visit: about 2 min.
The PT comes from the next room, reexamines her and arranges the emergency department: about 10 min.
Arranging transport to the emergency department: about 10 min.

why.question: What has changed for Ms. Alvarez, and what do you do with today's session?

parts.label: What the data show
parts.criteria: New urinary hesitancy, saddle numbness and new weakness and reflex loss in both legs: red-flag features of possible cauda equina compression, not a routine flare.
parts.modelAnswer: She has new difficulty starting to urinate, numbness when wiping, and both ankles are weaker with reduced reflexes. Those are red flags for cauda equina compression, not part of her usual back pain.

parts.label: What I do and who decides
parts.criteria: Holds all treatment (no traction, no exercise); tells the supervising PT at once with the objective data; the PT reexamines and decides the referral; documents data, not a diagnosis.
parts.modelAnswer: I stop the session: no traction and no exercise. I get Dr. Kim now and give her the data. Reexamination and the referral are her decisions; I document what I found, who I told and when.

expertPath.text: Check-in: back better, but new tingling in both legs.
The plan's red-flag screen: urinary hesitancy and saddle numbness since last night.
Strength, sensation and reflexes: weaker on both sides. No treatment.
Get the PT now with the data. Note the findings as data and document the hand-off.

retention.headline: Retention in the clinic
retention.body: Run the plan's bladder, bowel and saddle screen before treating, and never load the spine once a red flag appears.

delayed.headline: Sent home with red flags unreported
delayed.body: A new red flag is not something to save for the reexamination. The PTA stops and tells the supervising PT before going on.

ptNow.headline: Held and reported
ptNow.body: You screened before treating, held the session, collected the data the plan allows and told the PT within minutes. The PT reexamined and decided. That is the expert path.

sentGaps.headline: Sent, with gaps
sentGaps.body: Check whether treatment loaded her spine first, how long it took to tell someone, and whether the PT, who reexamines and decides, was in the loop.

time_up.headline: Still in the clinic
time_up.body: A new red flag needs the PT within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: New urinary hesitancy, saddle numbness and new weakness with reduced reflexes in both legs are red flags for cauda equina compression. A PTA does not reexamine, diagnose or change the plan, but stops the intervention for safety and tells the supervising PT at once with objective data. The PT reexamines and sends her for an emergency MRI. Traction or exercise in the meantime loads a compressed cauda equina, and saving it for the reexamination at visit 8 risks permanent harm.

Morning stiffness that eases with movement

cesQ.explain: New urinary retention, bowel dysfunction, saddle anesthesia or bilateral leg weakness is possible cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency.
